blocks.text: Pulp fantasy aesthetic is a design aesthetic that was prevalent from 1960s to 1970s that features muscular heroism, raw, exotic, kitschy landscapes, and a retro-sensationalism as a distinct element. It was heavily popularized by the progressive rock, sci-fi media, imaginative fantasy, paperback art and album covers and was rooted in the cheaply, airbrushed, printed "pulp" magazines where this aesthetic diffuses dramatic chiaroscuro lighting, intense action, primal, and an untamed magic.

The aesthetic focuses heavily on surreal, moody environments beyond individual heroes, with blood-red twin moons, looming monolithic citadels, untamed primordial jungles where ancient science and cosmic horror bleed into myth, and eerie glowing caverns, along with the single biggest influencers such as Frank Frazetta, whose oil-painted, dynamic compositions portrayed the appearance of John Carter of Mars and Conan the Barbarian. His work incorporates visceral motion, hyper-muscular figures, surrealistic, smoky, and atmospheric backgrounds, dominated by distressed, bold typography, high-stakes action scenes and lurid colors, magazine covers and classic book that feature the dangerous, gritty essence of the genre where publications such as Weird Tales discovered a visual formula of a way to dare monstrous foes, perilous enchantments and warriors.
